Oh, don’t be so cruel. I’m not fit to die. I will never bite anyone again. I will tell the truth. I will do good. Is it my fault if I was not made properly? Kill him; but spare me.
No! I have done no harm: she has. Kill her if you like: you have no right to kill me.
Do you hear that? They want to have one another killed.
Kill us both. How could either of us live without the other?
The woman is more sensible than the man.
I think it would be nice to give the poor things a little music.
I don’t know. But it would.
She rises on her knees and looks raptly into space.
Crawling feebly towards her until he reaches her hand.
The music stops. There is dead silence for a moment.
It was. Even the Ancients are smiling.
Quickly recovering her grave and peremptory manner.
Some of them move to obey.
Or the wind from the sea at the turn of the tide!

The air will be clean in a moment. This doll flesh that children make decomposes quickly at best; but when it is shaken by such passions as the creatures are capable of, it breaks up at once and becomes horribly tainted.
Let it be a lesson to you all to be content with lifeless toys, and not attempt to make living ones. What would you think of us ancients if we made toys of you children?

It would not amuse us. When you play with one another you play with your bodies, and that makes you supple and strong; but if we played with you we should play with your minds, and perhaps deform them.
You are a ghastly lot, you ancients. I shall kill myself when I am four years old. What do you live for?
You will find out when you grow up. You will not kill yourself.
If you make me believe that, I shall kill myself now.
Oh no. I want you. I love you.
I love someone else. And she has gone old, old. Lost to me forever.
You saw her when you barged into us as we were dancing. She is four.
How I should have hated her twenty minutes ago! But I have grown out of that now.
Good. That hatred is called jealousy, the worst of our childish complaints.

Ancients: I should like to make a few studies of you. Not portraits, of course: I shall idealize you a little. I have come to the conclusion that you ancients are the most interesting subjects after all.
What! Have those two horrors, whose ashes I have just deposited with peculiar pleasure in poor Pygmalion’s dustbin, not cured you of this silly image-making!

Why did you model them as young things, you fool? If Pygmalion had come to me, I should have made ancients of them for him. Not that I should have modelled them any better. I have always said that no one can beat you at your best as far as handwork is concerned. But this job required brains. That is where I should have come in.

Well, my brainy boy, you are welcome to try your hand. There are two of Pygmalion’s pupils at the laboratory who helped him to manufacture the bones and tissues and all the rest of it. They can turn out a couple of new automatons; and you can model them as ancients if this venerable pair will sit for you.
Only fancy, Acis! Arjillax wants to make more of those abominable things, and to destroy even their artistic character by making ancients of them.
You won’t sit for them, will you? Please don’t.
For heaven’s sake don’t tell us that the earth was once inhabited by Ozymandiases and Cleopatras. Life is hard enough for us as it is.
Life is not meant to be easy, my child; but take courage: it can be delightful. What I wanted to tell you is that ever since men existed, children have played with dolls.
You keep using that word. What are dolls, pray?
What you call works of art. Images. We call them dolls.
Just so. You have no sense of art; and you instinctively insult it.
Children have been known to make dolls out of rags, and to caress them with the deepest fondness.
Eight centuries ago, when I was a child, I made a rag doll. The rag doll is the dearest of all.
I kept it a full week.
Even in your childhood, then, you did not understand high art, and adored your own amateur crudities.
When you have lived as long as I have﻿—
You are still capable of thanking, though you do not know what you thank. You are a thanking little animal, a blaming little animal, a﻿—
And, as she thinks, an artistic little animal.

That is where you are wrong, my child. If those two loathsome things had been rag dolls, they would have been amusing and lovable. The Newly Born here would have played with them; and you would all have laughed and played with them too until you had torn them to pieces; and then you would have laughed more than ever.
Of course we should. Isn’t that funny?
When a thing is funny, search it for a hidden truth.
Yes; and take all the fun out of it.
Do not be so embittered because your sweetheart has outgrown her love for you. The Newly Born will make amends.
Oh yes: I will be more than she could ever have been.
Oh no. I have grown out of that. I love her now because she loved you, and because you love her.
That is the next stage. You are getting on very nicely, my child.
Come! what is the truth that was hidden in the rag doll?

Well, consider why you are not content with the rag doll, and must have something more closely resembling a real living creature. As you grow up you make images and paint pictures. Those of you who cannot do that make stories about imaginary dolls. Or you dress yourselves up as dolls and act plays about them.

And, to deceive yourself the more completely, you take them so very very seriously that Ecrasia here declares that the making of dolls is the holiest work of creation, and the words you put into the mouths of dolls the sacredest of scriptures and the noblest of utterances.

Yet the more beautiful they become the further they retreat from you. You cannot caress them as you caress the rag doll. You cannot cry for them when they are broken or lost, or when you pretend they have been unkind to you, as you could when you played with rag dolls.
At last, like Pygmalion, you demand from your dolls the final perfection of resemblance to life. They must move and speak.
They must think that they think.
They must have soft flesh and warm, blood.

And then, when you have achieved this as Pygmalion did; when the marble masterpiece is dethroned by the automaton and the homo by the homunculus; when the body and the brain, the reasonable soul and human flesh subsisting, as Ecrasia says, stand before you unmasked as mere machinery, and your impulses are shown to be nothing but reflexes, you are filled with horror and loathing, and would give worlds to be young enough to play with your rag doll again, since every step away from it has been a step away from love and happiness. Is it not true?
Speak, Martellus: you who have travelled the whole path.
It is true. With fierce joy I turned a temperature of a million degrees on those two things I had modelled, and saw them vanish in an instant into inoffensive dust.
Speak, Arjillax: you who have advanced from imitating the lightly living child to the intensely living ancient. Is it true, so far?
It is partly true: I cannot pretend to be satisfied now with modelling pretty children.
And you, Ecrasia: you cling to your highly artistic dolls as the noblest projections of the Life Force, do you not?
Without art, the crudeness of reality would make the world unbearable.

I am in my fourth year; and I have got on very well without your dolls. I had rather walk up a mountain and down again than look at all the statues Martellus and Arjillax ever made. You prefer a statue to an automaton, and a rag doll to a statue. So do I; but I prefer a man to a rag doll. Give me friends, not dolls.
Yet I have seen you walking over the mountains alone. Have you not found your best friend in yourself?
What are you driving at, old one? What does all this lead to?
It leads, young man, to the truth that you can create nothing but yourself.
It is as easy to understand as any other ignorant error. What artist is as great as his own works? He can create masterpieces; but he cannot improve the shape of his own nose.
There! What have you to say to that, old one?

He can alter the shape of his own soul. He could alter the shape of his nose if the difference between a turned-up nose and a turned-down one were worth the effort. One does not face the throes of creation for trifles.
What have you to say to that, Ecrasia?

I say that if the ancients had thoroughly grasped the theory of fine art they would understand that the difference between a beautiful nose and an ugly one is of supreme importance: that it is indeed the only thing that matters.
That is, they would understand something they could not believe, and that you do not believe.
Just so, mam. Art is not honest: that is why I never could stand much of it. It is all make-believe. Ecrasia never really says things: she only rattles her teeth in her mouth.
You mean that I won’t play the game of make-believe. Well, I don’t ask you to play it with me; so why should you expect me to play it with you?

You have no right to say that I am not sincere. I have found a happiness in art that real life has never given me. I am intensely in earnest about art. There is a magic and mystery in art that you know nothing of.

Yes, child: art is the magic mirror you make to reflect your invisible dreams in visible pictures. You use a glass mirror to see your face: you use works of art to see your soul. But we who are older use neither glass mirrors nor works of art. We have a direct sense of life. When you gain that you will put aside your mirrors and statues, your toys and your dolls.
Yet we too have our toys and our dolls. That is the trouble of the ancients.
What! The ancients have their troubles! It is the first time I ever heard one of them confess it.

Yes: this body is the last doll to be discarded. When I was a child, Ecrasia, I, too, was an artist, like your sculptor friends there, striving to create perfection in things outside myself. I made statues: I painted pictures: I tried to worship them.
I had no such skill; but I, like Acis, sought perfection in friends, in lovers, in nature, in things outside myself. Alas! I could not create if. I could only imagine it.

I, like Arjillax, found out that my statues of bodily beauty were no longer even beautiful to me; and I pressed on and made statues and pictures of men and women of genius, like those in the old fable of Michelangelo. Like Martellus, I smashed them when I saw that there was no life in them: that they were so dead that they would not even dissolve as a dead body does.

And I, like Acis, ceased to walk over the mountains with my friends, and walked alone; for I found that I had creative power over myself but none over my friends. And then I ceased to walk on the mountains; for I saw that the mountains were dead.
Mere metaphor, my poor boy: the mountains are corpses.

Yes. In the hardpressed heart of the earth, where the inconceivable heat of the sun still glows, the stone lives in fierce atomic convulsion, as we live in our slower way. When it is cast out to the surface it dies like deep-sea fish: what you see is only its cold dead body. We have tapped that central heat as prehistoric man tapped water springs; but nothing has come up alive from those flaming depths: your landscapes, your mountains, are only the world’s cast skins and decaying teeth on which we live like microbes.
Ancient: you blaspheme against Nature and against Man.

Child, child, how much enthusiasm will you have for man when you have endured eight centuries of him, as I have, and seen him perish by an empty mischance that is yet a certainty? When I discarded my dolls as he discarded his friends and his mountains, it was to myself I turned as to the final reality. Here, and here alone, I could shape and create. When my arm was weak and I willed it to be strong, I could create a roll of muscle on it; and when I understood that, I understood that I could without any greater miracle give myself ten arms and three heads.
I also came to understand such miracles. For fifty years I sat contemplating this power in myself and concentrating my will.

So did I; and for five more years I made myself into all sorts of fantastic monsters. I walked upon a dozen legs: I worked with twenty hands and a hundred fingers: I looked to the four quarters of the compass with eight eyes out of four heads. Children fled in amazement from me until I had to hide myself from them; and the ancients, who had forgotten how to laugh, smiled grimly when they passed.
We have all committed these follies. You will all commit them.
Oh, do grow a lot of arms and legs and heads for us. It would be so funny.
My child: I am just as well as I am. I would not lift my finger now to have a thousand heads.
But what would I not give to have no head at all?
What’s that? No head at all? Why? How?

One day, when I was tired of learning to walk forward with some of my feet and backwards with others and sideways with the rest all at once, I sat on a rock with my four chins resting on four of my palms, and four or my elbows resting on four of my knees. And suddenly it came into my mind that this monstrous machinery of heads and limbs was no more me than my statues had been me, and that it was only an automaton that I had enslaved.
A thing that must do what you command it is a slave; and its commander is its master. These are words you will learn when your turn comes.
You will also learn that when the master has come to do everything through the slave, the slave becomes his master, since he cannot live without him.
And so I perceived that I had made myself the slave of a slave.
When we discovered that, we shed our superfluous heads and legs and arms until we had our old shapes again, and no longer startled the children.
But still I am the slave of this slave, my body. How am I to be delivered from it?
That, children, is the trouble of the ancients. For whilst we are tied to this tyrannous body we are subject to its death, and our destiny is not achieved.
The day will come when there will be no people, only thought.
And that will be life eternal.
I trust I shall meet my fatal accident before that day dawns.
For once, Ecrasia, I agree with you. A world in which there were nothing plastic would be an utterly miserable one.

No limbs, no contours, no exquisite lines and elegant shapes, no worship of beautiful bodies, no poetic embraces in which cultivated lovers pretend that their caressing hands are wandering over celestial hills and enchanted valleys, no﻿—
Yes: inhuman. Why don’t you fall in love with someone?
I! I have been in love all my life. I burned with it even in the egg.
Not a bit of it. You and Arjillax are just as hard as two stones.
You did not always think so, Acis.
Oh, I know. I offered you my love once, and asked for yours.
And did I deny it to you, Acis?
You didn’t even know what love was.
Oh! I adored you, you stupid oaf, until I found that you were a mere animal.

And I made no end of a fool of myself about you until I discovered that you were a mere artist. You appreciated my contours! I was plastic, as Arjillax says. I wasn’t a man to you: I was a masterpiece appealing to your tastes and your senses. Your tastes and senses had overlaid the direct impulse of life in you. And because I cared only for our life, and went straight to it, and was bored by your calling my limbs fancy names and mapping me into mountains and valleys and all the rest of it, you called me an animal. Well, I am an animal, if you call a live man an animal.
You need not explain. You refused to be refined. I did my best to lift your prehistoric impulses on to the plane of beauty, of imagination, of romance, of poetry, of art, of﻿—

These things are all very well in their way and in their proper places. But they are not love. They are an unnatural adulteration of love. Love is a simple thing and a deep thing: it is an act of life and not an illusion. Art is an illusion.

That is false. The statue comes to life always. The statues of today are the men and women of the next incubation. I hold up the marble figure before the mother and say, “This is the model you must copy.” We produce what we see. Let no man dare to create in art a thing that he would not have exist in life.

Yes: I have been through all that. But you yourself are making statues of ancients instead of beautiful nymphs and swains. And Ecrasia is right about the ancients being inartistic. They are damnably inartistic.

The body always ends by being a bore. Nothing remains beautiful and interesting except thought, because the thought is the life. Which is just what this old gentleman and this old lady seem to think too.
A vortex. I began as a vortex: why should I not end as one?
Oh! That is what you old people are, Vorticists.
But if life is thought, can you live without a head?
Not now perhaps. But prehistoric men thought they could not live without tails. I can live without a tail. Why should I not live without a head?
A habit of which your ancestors managed to pure themselves.
None of us now believe that all this machinery of flesh and blood is necessary. It dies.
It imprisons us on this petty planet and forbids us to range through the stars.
But even a vortex is a vortex in something. You can’t have a whirlpool without water; and you can’t have a vortex without gas, or molecules or atoms or ions or electrons or something, not nothing.
No: the vortex is not the water nor the gas nor the atoms: it is a power over these things.
We are staying too long with you, children. We must go.
It is tiresome for us, too. You see, children, we have to put things very crudely to you to make ourselves intelligible.
And I am afraid we do not quite succeed.
Very kind of you to come at all and talk to us, I’m sure.
Why do the other ancients never come and give us a turn?
It is difficult for them. They have forgotten how to speak; how to read; even how to think in your fashion. We do not communicate with one another in that way or apprehend the world as you do.
I find it more and more difficult to keep up your language. Another century or two and it will be impossible. I shall have to be relieved by a younger shepherd.
Of course we are always delighted to see you; but still, if it tries you very severely, we could manage pretty well by ourselves, you know.
Tell me, Acis: do you ever think of yourself as having to live perhaps for thousands of years?
Oh, don’t talk about it. Why, I know very well that I have only four years of what any reasonable person would call living; and three and a half of them are already gone.
You must not mind our saying so; but really you cannot call being an ancient living.
I made up my mind on that subject long ago. When I am three years and fifty weeks old, I shall have my fatal accident. And it will not be an accident.
We are very tired of this subject. I must leave you.
The penalty of attending to children. Farewell.
Yet one would like to follow them; to enter into their life; to grasp their thought; to comprehend the universe as they must.
Well, I have finished with the dolls; and I am no longer jealous of you. That looks like the end. Two hours sleep is enough for me. I am afraid I am beginning to find you all rather silly.
I know. My girl went off this morning. She hadn’t slept for weeks. And she found mathematics more interesting than me.
He passes away gravely into the grove.
There goes a great spirit. What a sculptor he was! And now, nothing! It is as if he had cut off his hands.
Oh, will you all leave me as he has left you?
What is the use of swearing? She swore. He swore. You have sworn. They have sworn.
That is how one ought to speak, isn’t it? We shall all be forsworn.
Do not talk like that. You are saddening us; and you are chasing the light away. It is growing dark.
Night is falling. The light will come back tomorrow.
All begin trooping into the temple.
Silence. Little children should be seen and not heard.
Putting out her tongue at him.
Ungraceful. You must not do that.
I will do what I like. But there is something the matter with me. I want to lie down. I cannot keep my eyes open.
You are falling asleep. You will wake up again.
He takes her by the ear, and leads her firmly towards the temple.
Come, Arjillax: you at least are still an artist. I adore you.
Do you? Unfortunately for you, I am not still a child. I have grown out of cuddling. I can only appreciate your figure. Does that satisfy you?
He strides off into the temple.
She looks round, seeking another partner; but they have all gone.
The ghost of Adam, the first father of mankind. Who are you?
The ghost of Eve, the first mother of mankind.
Come forth, wife; and show yourself to me.
Who laughs? Who dares laugh at Adam?
Who has the heart to laugh at Eve?
He appears between them; and as he does so there is a prolonged hiss.
She becomes visible, coiled in the trees.
There is one that came before the serpent.
That is the voice of Lilith, in whom the father and mother were one. Hail, Lilith!
I suffered unspeakably; I tore myself asunder; I lost my life, to make of my one flesh these twain, man and woman. And this is what has come of it. What do you make of it, Adam, my son?
I made the earth bring forth by my labor, and the woman bring forth by my love. And this is what has come of it. What do you make of it, Eve, my wife?
I nourished the egg in my body and fed it with my blood. And now they let it fall as the birds did, and suffer not at all. What do you make of it, Cain, my firstborn?

I invented killing and conquest and mastery and the winnowing out of the weak by the strong. And now the strong have slain one another; and the weak live forever; and their deeds do nothing for the doer more than for another. What do you make of it, snake?
